div.p: These pages complement the extensive Visual Studio Code documentation that begins:
div.blockquote: Visual Studio Code is a lightweight but powerful source code editor which runs on your desktop and is available for Windows, macOS and Linux. It comes with built-in support for JavaScript, TypeScript and Node.js and has a rich ecosystem of extensions for other languages...
div.p: Visual Studio Code's user interface has a different look and feel to that of legacy XSLT editors. The Command Palette, along with keybindings to most common commands, play a significant role in providing a clearer environment to work in. User interface clutter is significantly reduced by eschewing previous designs which depended on a set of toolbars, each with an abundance of buttons.

The application menu bar and associated dropdown menus usefully group the more essential actions for managing your code. The View menu is particularly useful as it logically sets out the large set of view-configuration commands.
The sections below introduce you to the fundamental parts of the user interface from the perspective of an XSLT/XPath developer.

A principal part of Visual Studio Code's user interface is the Command Palette, triggered by the keyboard shortcut ⇧⌘P. The Command Palette shows all available commands in a dropdown list. The list of commands is filtered as you type. The most recently used commands are shown at the top of the list.

figcaption.i: VS Code's command palette - built in commands are supplemented by specialist XSLT/XML commands.

div.p: The File: Open Folder command is used to select the starting 'Workspace' folder to be used by VS Code. More folders can be added to the Workspace subsequently using the Workspaces: Add folder to workspace command. The keyboard shortcut ⌘P provides quick-access to all Workspace files from a pick-list. 'Fuzzy-matching' allows you to type in just a part of the filename to filter the pick-list files.

While the Command Palette provides convenient access to features you should find that keyboard shortcuts are more effective for commands you use most frequently. The keyboard shortcut for commands is shown alongside each listed command in the Command Palette. Not all commands have key bindings, but these can be configured using the command Preferences: Open Keyboard Shortcuts (⌘K⌘S). See: Key Bindings for Visual Studio Code

By adding or modifying Visual Studio Settings, using the Preferences: Open User Settings command, you can customize a range of editor and extension features to meet your needs. See the Settings section for details on some of the more important settings for developing in XSLT and XPath.
Extensions are managed in the Extensions view (⇧⌘X) of the Side Bar. Type XSLT XPath in the Extensions view search bar and, on the XSLT/XPath for Visual Studio Code entry, press the install button.

Visual Studio Code includes a small set of light and dark color themes. Alternative color themes are installed as extensions. The number of available themes can be overwhelming, but VS Code has a built-in Theme Preview feature and there are websites like vscodethemes that provide a preview before installing the theme.
The XSLT Dark Themes extension provides a set of popular dark color themes specially enhanced for XSLT and XPath
div.aside: The XSLT/XPath extension syntax highlighter uses Semantic Highlighting that should be enabled specifically in Settings to work with external color themes. Highlighter tokens are defined to provide effective highlighting for all the common color themes.
div.p: When your XSLT generates HTML, you can view the result in Visual Studio Code's integrated browser, with no extension needed. When a transform writes an HTML result file, the notification that the task has completed has an Open in Browser button, as well as Open for the file's source. You can also choose Open in Integrated Browser from the editor title bar of an HTML file, or from its context menu in the Explorer. With the workbench.browser.autoReloadOnFileChange setting, the page reloads each time the transform writes the result file again - so you can edit the stylesheet, run it with Quick Run, and see the updated output alongside the XSLT.
